Accountant Resume Example: Write an Accounting Resume That Passes the ATS in 2026

Accounting resumes pass through a finance team's checklist before a human ever reads them: license status, named ERP systems, proof you can close the books on time — and applicant tracking systems score all of it as plain text. "Assisted with month-end activities" tells the parser nothing: it can't tell whether you closed in 4 days or 14, or whether the ERP was NetSuite or a spreadsheet.

What gets shortlisted is proof: an active CPA license (or honest candidate status) up front, named ERP systems, reconciliation volumes, and outcomes with numbers — days shaved off the close, audit adjustments avoided, dollars saved. Below: a complete annotated example, plus the ATS rules for accounting hiring.

Quick answer: An accountant resume should include: CPA status (active license or candidate), named certifications, a 3-line summary with years and industry, quantified experience (month-end close time, reconciliation volume, cost savings), named ERP and Excel skills, education (B.S. Accounting), and keywords mirrored from the posting. Hiring software checks credentials first — duty lists without numbers get ranked down.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with your credential — CPA license (state, status) or "CPA candidate" with exam progress. Finance filters check this first.
  • Name your environment precisely: industry, company size, ERP (NetSuite, SAP, QuickBooks), and reporting scope.
  • Quantify close-cycle wins: close days, reconciliation volumes, audit adjustments, dollars saved or recovered.
  • Mirror the posting's exact terms — "reconciliations," "variance analysis," and "SOX" are distinct ATS keywords.
  • Keep formatting ATS-clean: single column, standard headings, no graphics, no tables, no creative section titles.

Accountant Resume Example (Annotated)

YOUR NAME
City, ST | (555) 555-0100 | youremail@email.com
linkedin.com/in/yourname

CERTIFICATION
CPA — [State], license active
CPA candidates: write "CPA candidate — 2 of 4 exams passed (target [year])" instead

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
Staff accountant with 5 years in manufacturing, closing the books for a $40M-revenue business unit. Cut month-end close from 8 days to 4 while reconciling 400+ balance-sheet accounts monthly; two consecutive external audits with zero adjustments. NetSuite and advanced Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP).

Why it works: license status first, years, industry, revenue scope, two metrics, ERP and Excel skills named literally — every claim a hiring manager can verify in an interview.

ACCOUNTING EXPERIENCE

Staff Accountant | [Firm] | 2021 – Present
• Cut month-end close from 8 days to 4 by rebuilding the close checklist and automating 12 recurring journal entries in NetSuite
• Reconcile 400+ balance-sheet accounts monthly; cleared a $2.1M backlog of unreconciled items within 90 days of joining
• Identified $180K in duplicate vendor payments during an AP cleanup; two consecutive external audits with zero adjustments
• Build monthly variance reports in Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP), reducing budget-review preparation from 3 days to 4 hours

Why it works: close days, account volumes, dollars recovered, named tools — the same proof-over-adjectives principle in our data analyst resume example.

Junior Accountant | [Firm] | 2019 – 2021
• Processed $1.5M in monthly accounts payable with 99.2% on-time payment; resolved invoice disputes with 40+ vendors
• Completed bank reconciliations for 12 operating accounts each month, flagging and clearing discrepancies within 5 business days
• Prepared audit schedules and PBC lists supporting a clean external audit

EDUCATION

Bachelor of Science in Accounting — [University] | 2019

ACCOUNTING SKILLS

GAAP, IFRS | month-end close, reconciliations, variance analysis, financial reporting, SOX compliance, accounts payable, accounts receivable, general ledger, budgeting, forecasting | NetSuite, QuickBooks, SAP, Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP)

What Employers and Hiring Software Scan For

The Jobscan 2026 ATS Usage Report puts ATS usage at 97.4% of Fortune 500 companies — and accounting roles get the same automated screening, since one posting can draw a flood of near-identical applicants. The software filters before any human reads your resume, scoring exact license, keyword, and tool matches.

Here's what both the software and the hiring manager look for, in priority order:

  1. Certification and license. Active CPA (state named) or honest CPA-candidate status. If the posting requires a CPA and your resume never says "CPA," you can be filtered out regardless of experience.
  2. Accounting context. Industry, company or business-unit size, reporting scope. "Staff accountant, $40M manufacturing business unit, NetSuite" says what you've handled; "did accounting" says nothing.
  3. ERP and Excel tools. NetSuite, SAP, QuickBooks — hiring teams search these terms literally, along with pivot tables and XLOOKUP. Standards and processes too: GAAP, IFRS, SOX compliance, variance analysis. Our accountant resume guide has more role-specific keyword lists.
  4. Outcomes with numbers. Close days, reconciliation volumes, audit adjustments, dollars saved — the same proof-over-adjectives principle in our nursing resume example.
  5. Keywords from the posting. Mirror exact terms. If the posting says "account reconciliations," write "account reconciliations," not "recs." The parser matches text, not intent.

New Accountant vs. Experienced Accountant Resume Structure

New accountants

  • Lead with CPA status and internships: license or exam progress, then placements — industry, ERP used, one quantified result per placement. Example: "Accounting intern, 6 months — QuickBooks; reconciled 50+ accounts monthly."
  • Candidate status is an asset. "CPA candidate — 2 of 4 exams passed" signals commitment; burying it looks like hiding.
  • Translate adjacent experience. Bookkeeping, AR/AP clerk work, or tax-season temp roles count — quantify volumes and deadlines met.

Experienced accountants (3+ years)

  • Lead with a 3-line summary (years, industry, scope, one metric), then reverse-chronological accounting experience.
  • Condense internships to one line under education, or drop them after 5+ years.
  • Show progression: close ownership, audit leadership, mentoring juniors.
  • Changing industries? Front-load transferable close-cycle skills in the summary so the screener sees the bridge.

The Exact Sections of an Accountant Resume

1. Certification

Always first for accounting. Format: CPA, state, active status — e.g., "CPA — [State], license active." Candidates write exam progress honestly. Never claim an inactive license as current.

2. Professional Summary (3 lines max)

Years + industry + scope + one metric. New accountants: lead with CPA status instead (e.g., "CPA candidate (2 of 4 exams passed); 6-month QuickBooks internship, 50+ accounts reconciled monthly.").

3. Accounting Experience

Reverse-chronological: title, firm, dates. Every bullet should carry at least one of: a close-cycle number, a volume, a named tool, or a dollar outcome. "Assisted with month-end" gets ignored; "Cut month-end close from 8 days to 4 in NetSuite" gets interviews.

4. Education

Degree, school, graduation year. New accountants can add relevant coursework; experienced accountants keep it to one line.

5. Accounting Skills

A scannable keyword list — name things literally: GAAP, IFRS, month-end close, reconciliations, variance analysis, SOX compliance, NetSuite, QuickBooks, SAP, Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP).

ATS Formatting Rules for Accountant Resumes

  • Single column, always. Two-column templates scramble parsing order — your certification can end up attributed to the wrong section. Pick a single-column ATS-friendly template.
  • Standard headings: Summary, Certification, Accounting Experience, Education, Accounting Skills. "My Ledger Journey" is invisible to the parser.
  • No tables, text boxes, or graphics. Accountants love tables, but parsers read them out of order or drop them. Plain text only.
  • Contact info in the body, not the header/footer. Many parsers skip headers and footers entirely.
  • Standard fonts, 10–12pt. Arial, Calibri, Georgia, Times New Roman.
  • File type: PDF unless the posting asks for .docx. Never Pages, image, or scanned files.
  • Length: one page under 5 years' experience; two pages max for experienced accountants. Cut oldest roles first, not the metrics.
  • Verify before you apply: run your resume through Cvyon's free ATS grader against the actual posting to catch parsing errors and keyword gaps.

7 Mistakes Accountants Make on Resumes

  1. Burying the CPA below the fold. Finance filters check credentials first — page two may never be read.
  2. Duty lists with no close numbers. "Helped with month end" matches nothing. "Cut month-end close from 8 days to 4 in NetSuite" matches the posting's requirements.
  3. Abbreviations without expansion. Write "Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)" and "Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX)" at least once — some systems index the full term, others the abbreviation.
  4. Creative section headings. "My Ledger Journey" doesn't map to the parser's expected sections. Use the standard five.
  5. Two-column "modern" templates. They look sharp and parse terribly — content order scrambles, and certifications can vanish.
  6. Missing the posting's exact credential term. The posting says "Certified Public Accountant" and you only wrote "CPA" — keyword score drops. Mirror their words.
  7. Vague CPA status. "CPA" with no state or status reads as careless — or as a claim the background check won't confirm.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in an accountant resume?

CPA status (active license with state, or candidate with exam progress); named certifications; a 3-line summary with years, industry, and scope; accounting experience with quantified results (close days, reconciliation volumes, audit adjustments, dollars saved); education (B.S. Accounting); and a skills section with standards (GAAP, IFRS), processes (month-end close, reconciliations, variance analysis, SOX), and named ERP and Excel tools. Every bullet should carry a number — days, volumes, or dollar outcomes.

How do I list a CPA vs. being a CPA candidate?

Active license: "CPA — [State], license active." Candidate: "CPA candidate — 2 of 4 exams passed (target [year])." Never write "CPA" alone if you are not licensed — hiring teams verify licenses. Candidate status is a strength early on, so put it first rather than hiding it.

How do I write an accountant resume with no experience?

Lead with CPA status and an Internship section: industry, ERP used, and one quantified result per placement (e.g., "Accounting intern, 6 months — QuickBooks; reconciled 50+ accounts monthly"). Add bookkeeping, AR/AP clerk, or tax-season temp work with numbers. Firms hire new accountants on license status and close-cycle exposure, not job titles.

How long should an accountant resume be?

One page for accountants under 5 years' experience; two pages maximum for experienced accountants. When trimming, cut older roles and redundant bullets — never the certification block, CPA status, or your strongest close-cycle metrics.

Do accountant resumes need to be ATS-friendly?

Yes — one posting can draw a flood of applicants with near-identical credentials, so software scores before a human reads your resume. Use a single-column layout, standard headings, certification first, exact license and ERP names, and keywords mirrored from the posting. Verify with Cvyon's free ATS grader before you apply.

Which skills and keywords should an accountant resume include?

GAAP, IFRS, SOX compliance; month-end close, reconciliations, variance analysis, financial reporting, budgeting, forecasting, general ledger, accounts payable and receivable; NetSuite, SAP, QuickBooks, Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP). Mirror the posting's exact terms — "reconciliations" and "recs" are different keywords to the parser.
